We deployed 26 specialized VAPI agents across operational workflows, connected them to a single 98-table Supabase instance (project ID: whxtjboruayowkqyjvcq) running 42 Edge Functions, and eliminated $8K+ monthly in SaaS overhead while cutting integration latency to sub-100ms. Here's what it actually cost to build, why the traditional startup stack failed at scale, and the exact architecture decisions that let one engineer operate six revenue streams from Day One.

entry.title: How I use a 10 MHz handheld oscilloscope for quick checks
entry.summary: I look after a small handheld oscilloscope here in the UK. It's the one I pick up for quick checks when setting up a bench scope isn't worth it. These are my notes on using it. The BSIDE OT3: a 10 MHz handheld digital oscilloscope with a 3.2" TFT screen and 48 MSa/s sampling, on one analogue channel. It runs on a built-in 3.7 V 1200 mAh battery and charges over USB Type-C. Long-press the power key to turn it on. Connect the BNC probe or the alligator-clip lead to the right-hand input. Clip ground to the circuit's ground, then put the probe tip on the signal. Press AUTO to scale the waveform. Use the direction keys to adjust timebase and volts per division by hand if AUTO isn't quite right. Slower signals sit comfortably inside 10 MHz: audio paths, PWM, and on cars things like injectors and crank or cam sensors. It isn't a 50 or 100 MHz bench scope, and fast digital edges above its rating won't look right, so I don't use it for those. Holding start/pause saves a screen image. The images come off over USB Type-C, and firmware updates use the same port. The menus are in Chinese and English. The probe uses a standard BNC connector, so a longer lead can be swapped in. It goes back on charge after a day of use rather than being left flat in the drawer. The scope I'm describing is the one on probeo.co.uk.
